Heart Posture
hart POS-cher
noun phrase
A modern evangelical coinage joining heart (the biblical seat of mind, will, and affections) with posture (a bodily stance, used figuratively for an inward disposition). 'Heart posture' names the inward attitude or bearing of the soul toward God or others — a soft, contemporary churchy phrase for an old biblical reality.

Biblical Verdict

🟡
Neutral
A sound idea in a soft phrase — safe when it names the obeying heart, risky when it spiritualizes feeling over obedience.

Biblical Definition

The reality behind the phrase is thoroughly biblical: God weighs the disposition of the heart, not merely the outward act. 'The LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart' (1 Sam. 16:7). He requires the inward bearing as well as the outward deed: 'this people draw near me with their mouth, and with their lips do honour me, but have removed their heart far from me' (Isa. 29:13). The heart is to be set, bowed, prepared: 'Ezra had prepared his heart to seek the law of the LORD' (Ezra 7:10); 'create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me' (Ps. 51:10); 'My son, give me thine heart' (Prov. 23:26). 'Heart posture,' rightly meant, names this inward stance — the bowed, humble, God-ward disposition that must underlie all true obedience. The substance is sound; only the phrase is modern.

Era

A soft modern churchy phrase for the disposition of the heart; basically sound (God weighs the heart, 1 Sam. 16:7) but often vague and used to spiritualize feelings over obedience.

HEART POSTURE, noun phrase. The inward attitude, disposition, or bearing of the soul toward God or others.

A modern evangelical coinage: heart (the biblical seat of mind, will, and affections) + posture (figurative inward stance).

Sound in substance: God looks on the heart (1 Sam. 16:7) and requires the inward disposition, not lip-service only (Isa. 29:13).

Cautioned in use: often vague, and sometimes deployed to elevate how one feels above what one is commanded to do.

Key Scripture

1 Samuel 16:7 — "But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart."

Proverbs 4:23 — "Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life."

Psalm 51:10 — "Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me."

Isaiah 29:13 — "Wherefore the Lord said, Forasmuch as this people draw near me with their mouth, and with their lips do honour me, but have removed their heart far from me, and their fear toward me is taught by the precept of men:"

Proverbs 23:26 — "My son, give me thine heart, and let thine eyes observe my ways."

Modern Corruption

Basically a sound notion — God weighs the heart — but the soft phrase is often vague, and is sometimes used to spiritualize feelings and disposition over actual obedience.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is subtler — a sound idea worn smooth by overuse and occasionally bent to excuse disobedience. 'Heart posture' rightly names what 1 Samuel 16:7 and Isaiah 29:13 establish: God is not content with the outward act but searches the inward disposition. So far it is wholesome. The first caution is mere vagueness: the phrase can become a pious filler, a way to sound spiritual ('I just want to check my heart posture') without the precision Scripture brings, which speaks of a clean heart, a contrite heart, a heart that keeps the commandments (Ps. 51:10, 17; John 14:15).

The graver misuse is to let inward 'posture' substitute for outward obedience — to treat having warm feelings toward God as if it were the same as doing what He says. Scripture binds the two: 'My son, give me thine heart, and let thine eyes observe my ways' (Prov. 23:26) — the given heart and the watched ways together. Christ rebukes the man who says 'Lord, Lord' with feeling but 'doeth not the things which I say' (Luke 6:46). A good 'heart posture' that does not issue in obedience is not the contrite heart God accepts but the lip-honour He rejects (Isa. 29:13). The phrase is safe only when the heart it describes is the heart that obeys.

The recovery is to keep heart and act welded as Scripture welds them. 'Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life' (Prov. 4:23) — the heart is guarded precisely because it issues in life and conduct. A right inward disposition is not an alternative to obedience but its spring; the bowed heart bows the body too. So the phrase may be kept, provided it is anchored: 'heart posture' means the God-ward, humble, repentant disposition that produces obedience — never a feeling that excuses its absence.

Hebrew Roots

A modern phrase for the heart's disposition; sound in substance (God looks on the heart, 1 Sam. 16:7) but to be kept precise and welded to obedience, never a feeling that excuses it.

expand to see more

English: heart (biblical seat of mind, will, affections) + posture (figurative inward stance) — a modern evangelical coinage.

Hebrew: the biblical leb / lebab, the whole inner man — what 1 Sam. 16:7 says the LORD beholds.

Biblical weld: Prov. 23:26 binds the given heart to the watched ways — disposition and obedience together, never apart.

Usage

"He spoke much of his 'heart posture' and little of his obedience, but the LORD who looks on the heart also said, 'keep my commandments.'"

"A bowed heart bows the body too; right disposition is obedience's spring, not its substitute."

"The phrase is safe when anchored: the God-ward, repentant heart that issues in doing what He says."
